title: Raga Ramkali
hook: a calm morning raga, home of Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis, that opens by setting learning aside for the one Name

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Gond: a frightened driver, a judge who didn't see, and your line, the elephant bowed. Did you take a second look at someone? A new week starts. Day one thousand one hundred.

Some read Sanskrit. Some read the old Puranas. Some sit with a string of beads, counting the Name, fixed in meditation. That's how today's raga begins, on ang eight seventy-six of the Guru Granth Sahib: a quick tour of serious religious people doing serious religious things. A listener might expect the next line to pick a winner. It doesn't. Guru Nanak steps out of the lineup altogether, and what he says next is very quiet. Today: Raga Ramkali.
screen: `SANSKRIT, PURANAS, BEADS.` → `A LINEUP OF THE DEVOUT.` → `NANAK STEPS OUT OF IT.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Ramkali follows Gond in the Granth's order, and Sikh tradition hears it as a calm morning raga. Second, the opening hymn's turn, in paraphrase: I know nothing, now or ever; I recognize only your one Name. Then the refrain: I don't know, Lord, what my state is. And then: I'm foolish and without understanding; I've come to your shelter; be kind, and keep my honor. Notice the move. No reader is mocked, no bead-counter is scorned. Guru Nanak simply doesn't compete. Where others show what they know, he admits what he doesn't, and rests in the Name. That's the calm. Third, the yogis. Ramkali is where the Granth holds Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis, the wandering ascetics with their earrings, horns and begging bags; tomorrow we'll open the Sidh Gosht, his long conversation with them. In another of his Ramkali hymns, in paraphrase, Guru Nanak takes up their own gear: awareness of the Word is my horn, and the world hears it sound; honor is my begging bag, and the Name is the alms I receive. Tradition says the yogis honored a master called Gorakh. The hymn's refrain answers: the true Gorakh is the One who lifted up the earth and made it without delay. Fourth, put it together. In Ramkali, the outward signs of religion, scholarship, beads, earrings, horns, are each turned inward and pointed at the Name. Nothing is thrown away; everything goes deeper. That's today's line: calm and deep.
screen: `RAMKALI FOLLOWS GOND.` · `I RECOGNIZE ONLY YOUR ONE NAME.` · `THE WORD IS MY HORN.` · `EVERY OUTWARD SIGN TURNED INWARD.` · then, large: `CALM AND DEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Ramkali, or step out of the lineup. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Ramkali, ideally in the morning. If not, sit and let the breath slow until it's barely noticeable. Then let go of whatever you know, for two minutes: what you've read, what you believe, what you'd argue for. Don't throw any of it away. Just set it down beside you. Sit with one word, or with nothing at all, the way a still lake sits under the morning. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be that one word. If you don't, let the breath be the horn the world hears. The bell holds the time.
Raga Ramkali. The calm morning raga after Gond, home of Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis, which opens with I recognize only your one Name. Today's word.
Your line: calm and deep. Today, the next time a conversation turns into who knows more, step out of it quietly, and let one deep breath answer instead. Day one thousand one hundred.

howItsDone: Shabads from the Ramkali section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan in Raga Ramkali, which Sikh musical tradition associates with a calm morning mood.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm raga is just slow music.
what it means: Ramkali's calm is not competing: setting knowledge down and resting in the one Name.
what a scholar hears: Ramkali (from ang 876) opens with Guru Nanak declining a contest of learning, and elsewhere turns the yogis' horn, bag and alms, and their master Gorakh, toward the Name.
recall: a musical instruction in the heading
